name: Metolazone

card.summary: A potent thiazide-like diuretic mostly used alongside loop diuretics in heart failure; no appearance data exists.
card.note: Strong prescription diuretic; can cause marked electrolyte depletion.

quick.overview:
Metolazone is a potent thiazide-like diuretic used for edema from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease, and sometimes for high blood pressure. Clinicians often pair it with a loop diuretic when the loop diuretic alone is insufficient.

It appears in this wiki as a strong water pill. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other cosmetic aims.
quick.mechanism: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, so less sodium and water return to the blood. It remains active at lower kidney function than most thiazides and is described as about ten times as potent as hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
quick.risks: Fluid loss can cause low blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalances (low sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium; high calcium and uric acid) are common concerns. Rare serious effects include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancreatitis and angioedema. It is prescription-only.[1]

lead: Metolazone is a prescription thiazide-like diuretic, sold as Zaroxolyn, Zytanix, Mykrox and Metoz, that helps the body shed salt and water. Its approved uses are edema from heart failure and kidney disease and high blood pressure, and it is often paired with a loop diuretic such as furosemide when fluid retention persists.[1][3]

In an appearance context, diuretics come up because they reduce water retention, the fluid that can make the face, hands and ankles look puffy. Metolazone is the strongest of these in everyday medical use, and it is mentioned on athletic banned-substance lists that circulate in strength-training forums.[1][9] The route to a leaner or less puffy look is therefore through lowering extracellular fluid, and it is a drug that clinicians generally supervise with blood tests because of its effects on electrolytes.[3]
Published research on metolazone concerns heart failure, kidney disease and hypertension. No trial has tested it for facial puffiness or physique outcomes.

chain: Blocks sodium-chloride reabsorption in the kidney
More sodium and water leave in the urine
Less retained fluid, so tissues look less swollen
angle.text: Metolazone increases urinary loss of salt and water, which reduces fluid retention in people with edema. It is a prescription medicine used under clinical monitoring, and it is not a cosmetic product.

paras: The US label lists metolazone for salt and water retention, including edema accompanying congestive heart failure and kidney disease such as nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension alone or with other antihypertensives. The rapidly available Mykrox formulation was intended for new patients with mild to moderate hypertension.[3] It is also used for edema from cirrhosis.[1]

Metolazone is frequently combined with a loop diuretic in what clinicians call sequential nephron blockade, when loop diuretics alone have stopped producing enough urine. Grokipedia says the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline supports adding a thiazide-type agent such as metolazone for refractory edema.[2]

Because it removes retained water, people who track weight or look for a drier, less swollen appearance sometimes ask about diuretics. T Nation threads that mention metolazone are lists of banned substances for the NFL, NCAA and school wrestling, where diuretics are prohibited because they can mask other drugs and cut weight quickly.[9][10][11] The Wikipedia entry places metolazone in the category of WADA-prohibited substances.[1]

Trials in heart failure have measured how much fluid or sodium is removed. The 3T trial randomised 60 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure and resistance to intravenous loop diuretics to oral metolazone, intravenous chlorothiazide or tolvaptan, all with high-dose furosemide. Weight loss at 48 hours was 4.6 kg with metolazone, 5.8 kg with chlorothiazide and 4.1 kg with tolvaptan, with no significant differences between them; all three improved diuretic efficacy.[5]

The DEA-HF study was a randomised, open-label crossover trial of 42 ambulatory chronic heart failure patients who each received three regimens: intravenous furosemide, furosemide plus oral metolazone, and furosemide plus intravenous acetazolamide. Over six hours, furosemide plus metolazone produced the highest sodium excretion, 4,691 mg, versus 3,835 mg for furosemide alone and 3,584 mg for the acetazolamide combination.[6]

A 1994 randomised trial examined combination diuretic treatment in severe heart failure,[4] and a narrative review of diuretic strategies in acute decompensated heart failure notes that the evidence for guiding combinations is limited and has relied on expert opinion and older landmark trials.[7] Earlier trials from the early 1970s studied metolazone for hypertension and for high-dose use in chronic renal failure.[12][13]

The label describes most adverse reactions as mild and transient and as extensions of the drug's pharmacology, such as volume depletion and orthostatic hypotension.[3] Electrolyte disturbances are the central concern: low sodium, potassium, chloride and magnesium and high calcium and uric acid, which can cause weakness, cramps, dizziness, headache or heart rhythm irregularities.[1][3] The label warns that severe low sodium or potassium has rarely appeared rapidly after initial doses of thiazide and non-thiazide diuretics.[3]

Rare serious effects include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancreatitis and angioedema; the drug may unmask diabetes or worsen gout, and people allergic to sulfonamides may react.[1] A review of drug-induced pancreatitis lists metolazone among agents with a questionable association.[14] Case reports describe BRASH syndrome, a combination of bradycardia, kidney injury and high potassium, in people on diuretics.[15]
Animal studies at doses up to 50 mg/kg/day found no fetal harm, but the label notes that no adequate trials exist in pregnant women and that metolazone crosses the placenta.[3]

Metolazone blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, so more sodium, chloride and water remain in the urine.[1][2] It is described as about ten times as potent as hydrochlorothiazide and, unlike most thiazides, remains active when kidney filtration is reduced.[1]

About 65 percent of an oral dose reaches the bloodstream. The half-life is roughly 14 hours, and about 80 percent is excreted in urine with little metabolism.[1] Grokipedia gives peak plasma levels at 2 to 4 hours.[2]

Metolazone was patented in 1966 and approved for medical use in 1974, according to Wikipedia, which credits the Indian-born chemist Bola Vithal Shetty with its development. It became popular partly because it appeared less harmful to the kidneys than thiazides in chronic kidney disease.[1] Grokipedia dates its first US approval to 1973 under the brand Zaroxolyn.[2]

Metolazone is available as a generic prescription medicine in the United States and is sold under several brand names.[1][3] Diuretics as a class appear on the banned lists of the WADA, the NFL and the NCAA, which the T Nation threads reproduce for athletes and wrestlers.[1][9][10][11]

Registered trials continue to compare metolazone with other add-on diuretics in acute decompensated heart failure, including a 320-patient trial against acetazolamide that began recruiting in 2025.[16] Earlier pilot studies, such as the MELT-HF trial of early metolazone add-on therapy, were terminated.[17]

No studies found on metolazone for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Human trials in heart failure include the 3T and DEA-HF randomised trials described above,[5][6] a randomised comparison of dapagliflozin and metolazone in loop-diuretic-resistant heart failure,[8] and the terminated MELT-HF pilot of early add-on therapy.[17]

timeline.event: British Medical Journal publishes a controlled study of high-dose metolazone in chronic renal failure.[13]
Approved for medical use per Wikipedia; antihypertensive trials reported.[1][12]
Randomised trial of combination diuretic treatment in severe heart failure.[4]
3T trial compares add-on diuretic strategies for loop diuretic resistance.[5]
DEA-HF crossover trial reports sodium excretion with furosemide plus metolazone.[6]

lore.intro: Metolazone shows up on T Nation mainly in copied lists of drugs banned by sports bodies, not in discussion of using it for looks.[9][10][11]

claims.claim: Diuretics such as metolazone can cut water weight quickly.
claims.believers: Athletes and lifters discuss banned-substance lists that include diuretics, which are known for making weight and for masking other drugs.[9][10]
claims.experts: Trials show metolazone increases sodium and urine output and weight loss in heart failure patients,[5][6] and the label warns of electrolyte depletion and volume depletion.[3] No study has tested it in healthy people for appearance.
